title: Sh-A-L
hook: sha'al, to ask; she'elah, a question

segments.voice: Yesterday, A-Ch-D: echad, one, the Shema's last word. Your line was one. A new week starts with a question, and the seder's four children, from day six hundred seventy-nine, come back.

A woman named Hannah is praying in the sanctuary at Shiloh, so hard that her lips move but no sound comes out, and the priest thinks she's drunk. She isn't. She's asking for a child. In time she has a son, and the text gives her own explanation of his name: she "called his name Samuel, saying, Because I have asked him of the LORD." Asked is she'iltiv, from the root sha'al. The prophet's whole life starts as an answer to someone's question.
screen: `HANNAH PRAYS WITHOUT A SOUND.` → `A SON NAMED SAMUEL.` → `I HAVE ASKED HIM OF THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Sh-A-L. Shin, alef, lamed. Sha'al: to ask. She'elah: a question. First, asking after someone. Joseph, now a ruler in Egypt, sees his brothers again, and they don't yet know who he is. When they bow to him, the text says: "he asked them of their welfare." In Hebrew, he asked them for shalom, and then about their old father. Here asking isn't only for information. It's how you reach for someone. Second, the table. The Torah expects children to ask: "when your children shall say unto you, What mean ye by this service?" The Passover seder is built around that. The youngest asks why this night is different. The Haggadah imagines four kinds of children, and one of them doesn't know how to ask at all. For that child, it says, you open the conversation yourself. A question is so central that if it's missing, someone has to start one. Third, the library. For centuries, when Jews had a hard question about how to live, they wrote to a rabbi, and the rabbi wrote back. Those letters are called she'elot u'teshuvot: questions and answers. Whole shelves of Jewish law grew out of people asking. In this tradition, a question isn't a sign you're lost. It's how the conversation stays alive.
screen: `JOSEPH ASKS AFTER THEIR SHALOM.` · `WHAT MEAN YE BY THIS SERVICE?` · `THE CHILD WHO CAN'T ASK.` · `SHE'ELOT U'TESHUVOT: LETTERS ASKING.` · then, large: `THE QUESTION KEEPS IT ALIVE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person you see often and rarely ask about, and notice what you don't know: where they grew up, what their week has been like, what they're carrying. Let one simple question take shape, the way Joseph asked after his brothers' shalom, and hold it quietly, the way Hannah held hers, lips barely moving. If you pray, you can pray for that person's shalom too.
screen: `ONE PERSON YOU SEE OFTEN.` · `ONE THING YOU DON'T KNOW.` · `SHAPE THE QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Sh-A-L. Shin, alef, lamed: the root of sha'al, to ask, and she'elah, a question, the word inside Hannah's naming of Samuel. Today's word.
Your line: ask. Hannah asked, and a prophet came; someone wrote in, and the law grew. Day one thousand four hundred eight, done.

howItsDone: At the Passover seder the youngest child traditionally asks why this night is different, and Jews bring hard questions of practice to a rabbi; the written exchanges are called she'elot u'teshuvot, questions and answers.

chat.says: At my friend's seder, a kid asked questions all night. Isn't that a bit disrespectful?
options: Not at all: the seder is built for questions, and if a child can't ask, you start one.
A little: only the youngest may ask, and just the four set questions.
It's fine, but questions really belong to the rabbis, not the family table.
